intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: Grade 12 is “geography of Eritrea in depth”. Grade 11 is the toolkit: how the crust moves, how water and wind carve, how people settle, then a first look at Eritrea’s place, relief and contour maps. Read each unit as a *story with a cause* — examiners mark the cause, not only the landform name.

intro_cards.title: Worked contour gradient
body: Two points: 1 200 m and 1 000 m. Map distance between them is 4 cm. Scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m).
Rise = 200 m. Run = 4 × 500 = 2 000 m. Gradient = 200/2000 = 1 in 10 (or 10%). Write both the fraction and a sentence: “For every 10 m walked horizontally you climb 1 m.”

units.title: Cultural Impact on the Natural Environment
units.intro:
Culture here means how people use the land: farming, herding, cutting wood, building cities, burning fuel. The physical environment offers limits (rain, slope, soil); culture can respect those limits or push them until the system snaps.

**Deforestation.** Trees are cut for fuel, construction, charcoal and new fields. Without roots and canopy, rain hits bare soil, runoff rises, rivers silt, springs weaken, local climate gets harsher. In Eritrea this is tightly tied to energy poverty (Unit 12 Ag / Geo 12 forests).

cards.title: 5.1 Understanding the Natural Environment
body: Human beings exist within a specific environment, which they have modified through activities such clearing of forests, building of roads and settlements.
Ancient people had very limited effects on the natural environment.
With the development of agriculture and industry, changes on the environment increased rapidly.
Modern technology has changed the relationships between people and their natural surroundings.
The most significant of these are the growth in world population and advancement in modern technology.

cards.title: The natural environment
body: The **natural environment** is made up of the atmosphere (air, climate), lithosphere (rocks, soil, landforms), hydrosphere (water) and biosphere (plants and animals). They interact all the time: for example, climate controls which plants grow, plants protect the soil, and soil and water support animals and people. A change in one part (such as cutting down forests) affects all the others.

cards.title: Explain why human impact on the environment has increased
cards.problem: Explain why early human societies had little effect on the natural environment, while modern societies change it greatly.

steps.text: **Step 1: Early societies.** Populations were small and tools were simple (stone tools, fire), so only small areas were cleared and nature recovered quickly.
**Step 2: Population growth.** As populations grew, more land was cleared and cultivated; in poorer countries even steep slopes are farmed and animals overgraze the vegetation.
**Step 3: Technology.** Modern machines, fossil fuels and industry let people change large areas quickly and produce pollution and hazardous by-products.
**Step 4: Link.** Impact = number of people × how much each uses × the technology used.
**Conclusion:** larger populations and powerful technology explain the much greater modern impact.

cards.answer: Early societies were small and used simple tools; today larger populations and modern technology (machines, fossil fuels, industry) let people clear, farm and pollute far larger areas.

cards.why: While all organisms interact with their environment, human beings have the most profound and large-scale impact through activities like industrialization, deforestation, urbanization, and pollution, leading to global environmental changes.

lessons.title: Humans as Modifiers of the Natural Environment

cards.title: Humans as Modifiers of the Natural Environment
body: **Desertification.** Productive dryland loses vegetation and soil until it behaves like desert. Causes are usually mixed: drought + too many animals on the same range + ploughing fragile soil + tree cutting. It is not a simple “desert advancing like a wall”. Reversing it means rest (enclosures), controlled grazing, and putting cover back.

**Global warming.** Extra greenhouse gases (CO₂ from fossil fuel and from lost forest, methane from livestock and waste) trap more outgoing heat. Effects that matter locally: more erratic rain, hotter lowlands, stress on already marginal farms.

**Acid rain and air pollution.** Sulphur and nitrogen oxides from industry and vehicles dissolve in rain and damage plants, water and stone. Cities add smoke, dust and traffic fumes. Even without giant factories, charcoal and diesel can foul a valley.

cards.title: Exam habit
body: Always pair a human cause with a physical result: “overgrazing → bare soil → wind/water erosion → lower yields.” One-word answers (“pollution”) score poorly.

cards.title: Who is most exposed?
body: Pastoral lowlands feel drought and desertification first. Highland slopes feel deforestation as gullies. Coastal towns feel heat, salt and any sea-level talk. A good essay names a belt, a process, and one practical response already in later books: terrace, enclosure, stove that uses less wood, managed grazing.

cards.title: Revision checklist (say these out loud)
body: - Desertification ≠ a marching dune wall; it is cover and soil lost on dryland.

cards.title: How people change the environment
body: People modify the environment to meet their needs: clearing forests for farmland and fuel, building terraces and dams, irrigating, mining, building towns and roads, and keeping livestock. Some changes help people (terraces conserve soil, dams store water), but careless use causes **soil erosion**, **deforestation**, **desertification**, loss of wildlife and pollution. Sustainable use means meeting today’s needs without harming the resources future generations will need.
In Eritrea, soil and water conservation (terracing, check dams) and tree planting are used to fight land degradation.

cards.title: Worked example: cause and effect chain
cards.problem: Explain how cutting trees on a hillside can lead to flooding downstream.

steps.text: Trees and their roots hold soil and slow rain water.
Without them, rain runs off quickly and carries soil away (erosion).

cards.answer: Rivers receive more water in a short time and fill with silt, so they **flood** more easily.

cards.problem: First step when describing a distribution map?

steps.text: Overall pattern, then anomalies, then data support.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All are major consequences of human impacts on the environment, except:
cards.why: **Strip cultivation** is a soil conservation method used by humans to **prevent** erosion. It is a positive action, unlike Global warming, desertification, and Acid rain, which are negative consequences (damages) to the environment.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The process of heat trapping by gases, which causes an increase in the average temperature of the world is?
cards.why: The **Greenhouse effect** is the physical process where certain gases (like $$CO_2$$ and methane) trap heat in the atmosphere. **Global warming** (D) is the resulting increase in temperature, but the *process* itself is called the greenhouse effect.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The relationship between people and the natural environment is described as "two-way" because ____.

options.C: the environment and people are not connected
options.D: people modify the environment, and the environment influences people's activities

cards.why:
**Step 1:** People change the environment, for example by clearing forests and building dams.

**Step 2:** The environment in turn limits or shapes what people can do, for example through rainfall, relief and soils.

**Step 3:** Influence in both directions is what "two-way" means.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

similar.q: Name two components of the natural environment.
similar.a: Air and water (also soil, forests, minerals).

similar.q: Is a dam part of the natural environment?
similar.a: No, it is part of the built (human) environment.

options.A: the roads and factories made by people
options.C: everything in nature, such as air, water, soil, forests and minerals, that affects living things
options.D: only the buildings in a town

why: Answer C: everything in nature, such as air, water, soil, forests and minerals, that affects living things
The natural environment includes all natural components that affect living things.
Its components include air, water, forest, soil and minerals.
Buildings, roads and factories are part of the human (built) environment.

Gases such as carbon dioxide trap heat in the atmosphere (the greenhouse effect).
Extra gases from burning fossil fuels increase this effect.
The result is a rise in global average temperature: global warming.
